metadata.title: Empowering schools’ improvement (EN) — Insights from PISA for Schools case studies

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA for Schools case-study synthesis is based on survey responses and multilingual in-depth interviews with school leaders and teachers, not on student microdata from PISA. The document reports counts of school responses (e.g., 366 responses across nine countries) and percentages of schools reporting actions, rather than estimating student-level achievement relationships. Because the analysis is qualitative/mixed-methods at the school level, complex survey weights and replicate-weight variance estimation (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are not described and are not applicable in the same way as for student-based ILSA achievement modeling. For any future quantitative re-analysis using PISA/PISA for Schools microdata, analysts should apply the official PISA/PISA for Schools sampling weights provided in the dataset and follow the replicate-weight procedure specified by the data provider; however, this report itself does not specify weight variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This publication does not conduct student-level achievement modeling with PISA Plausible Values (PVs). Instead, it synthesizes school-level survey responses and in-depth interview evidence to identify thematic categories and illustrative case-study patterns. As a result, PV handling and a formal missing-data strategy for PV-based outcomes are not part of the reported methodology; the missing-data handling is therefore not documented in the text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report describes a PISA for Schools Case Studies Research Project in collaboration with Oxford University. It states that 366 responses were collected across nine countries that voluntarily participated in the survey, combining survey responses with multilingual in-depth interviews with school leaders and teachers. It also states that ten case studies from six countries were selected to illustrate how schools translated data into change. The document does not list the nine countries explicitly in the provided text, nor does it specify any student-level inclusion/exclusion criteria because the analysis is not based on student microdata.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus report summarizes insights from PISA for Schools case studies rather than estimating statistical relationships from student achievement data. It explains that PISA for Schools (introduced in 2012) provides participating schools with confidential, school-level benchmarking aligned with PISA’s framework, covering performance in mathematics, reading, and science for 15-year-olds, and also addressing student motivation, perceptions of the school environment, and equity and inclusion. The case-study project collected 366 survey responses across nine countries and used multilingual in-depth interviews with school leaders and teachers to understand how schools interpret results and use them for decision-making and change. The report identifies four thematic categories describing how schools use the data and reports descriptive shares of schools implementing interventions, collaborating in networks, and viewing PISA for Schools as a catalyst for change. Methodologically, it emphasizes that data alone is insufficient without collective interpretation support, external feedback, monitoring tools, and professional development.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a descriptive synthesis of school-level case studies and survey/interview evidence, not an empirical predictive modeling study using ILSA microdata. Consequently, there is no student-level analytic sample size, no PV-based outcome modeling, no ML algorithm evaluation, and no reported predictive performance metrics. The report also does not enumerate the specific nine countries in the provided text, so per-country sample sizes cannot be extracted from the manuscript body.
